title: Encrypted Content-Encoding for HTTP
summary: Introduces an HTTP content coding that allows message payloads to be encrypted. A client or server can apply it to the body so the content is protected end to end beyond the transport.

eli5.summary: The body of a web message is put in a locked box. Only someone with the right key can open it.

questions: what is the aes128gcm content coding
how does http content encryption work
difference between tls and http content encryption
what is the record size in rfc 8188
subtitle: An HTTP content coding that encrypts the message body in fixed-size records, so stored or relayed content stays unreadable without the key.

tldr.problem: TLS only protects the channel between a client and a server. A file stored with an HTTP PUT, or copied to other servers, is exposed to whoever holds it.
tldr.mechanism: The aes128gcm content coding splits the body into fixed-size records, pads them and encrypts each with AEAD_AES_128_GCM. A small header carries the salt, record size and an optional key identifier, and the key and nonces are derived with HKDF.
tldr.outcome: A server can store and replicate content without being able to read it. Key management is left out, and only the body is protected, so headers and sizes can still leak information.

today: RFC 8188 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2017, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. The aes128gcm coding is registered in the HTTP Content Coding Registry.

sections.title: Why Encrypt the Body Itself
sections.content:
Sometimes the contents of an HTTP request or response should be readable only by someone holding the right key, even after the payload is stored (for example with an HTTP PUT). One example in the RFC is storing a file on a server without exposing its contents to that server, while the same file may be replicated to other servers or downloaded for offline use.

Transport Layer Security (TLS) does not meet this need, because it only encrypts the channel between client and server. This RFC defines a content coding instead: a transformation applied to the message body itself.

The format is not an adaptation of message-based encryption formats such as OpenPGP, CMS, JWE or XML Encryption, because those are not suited to the stream processing HTTP needs. It follows the lower-level constructs of RFC 5116. The RFC also says plainly that this is only a small part of a larger design: how clients and servers acquire and identify keys depends on the use case, and no key management system is described.
sections.eli5: Normal web security only protects the delivery truck. This puts the parcel itself in a locked box, so it stays private even when it sits in a warehouse.

sections.title: Records and the aes128gcm Coding
sections.content:
The aes128gcm content coding says the payload was encrypted with AES in Galois/Counter Mode, identified as AEAD_AES_128_GCM in RFC 5116, using a 128-bit content-encryption key. It uses one fixed set of primitives. Cipher agility comes from defining a new content coding, so the HTTP Accept-Encoding header field is all that is needed to negotiate encryption.

The encoded body is a header followed by zero or more fixed-size encrypted records. The final record can be smaller. Each record holds a piece of plaintext, then a single padding delimiter octet, then any number of zero octets. The delimiter is 1 in every record except the last, which uses 2. AEAD_AES_128_GCM makes the ciphertext 16 octets longer than the plaintext, so a valid record holds at least the delimiter and a 16-octet authentication tag.

On decryption, the delimiter is the last non-zero octet of the record. A decrypter MUST fail if a record has no non-zero octet, if the last record has a delimiter other than 2, or if any other record has a delimiter other than 1. The additional data passed to each encryption is a zero-length sequence.

Record size is a trade-off. Smaller records release decrypted octets sooner and make random access cheaper. Larger records, or a single record, reduce processing and data overhead. Range requests work at the granularity of the record size, because partial records at the ends of a range cannot be decrypted.
sections.eli5: The message is cut into equal-sized chunks, and each chunk goes into its own locked envelope. A little mark inside says whether it is the last chunk, so nobody can quietly cut the end off.

sections.title: The Coding Header
sections.content:
A header block at the start of the body holds every parameter needed to decrypt except the key. It has four parts:

  • salt: 16 octets. The same salt MUST NOT be reused for two different bodies with the same input-keying material. A random salt for every use makes key reuse highly unlikely.
  • rs: the record size, an unsigned 32-bit integer in network byte order. Values smaller than 18 are invalid.
  • idlen: an unsigned 8-bit integer giving the length of keyid.
  • keyid: optional identifier of the keying material. Recipients are expected to know how to retrieve keys, and this value may be input to that. It SHOULD be a UTF-8 string.
sections.eli5: The header is the label on the outside of the box. It says how big each chunk is and which key to try, but it never contains the key.

sections.title: Deriving the Key and Nonces
sections.content:
To let the same keying material protect many messages, a fresh content-encryption key is derived for each one with HKDF (RFC 5869) using SHA-256. The salt from the header is the HKDF salt, and the keying material named by keyid is the input-keying material (IKM), which must be supplied to recipients separately.

  • PRK = HMAC-SHA-256(salt, IKM)
  • CEK = HMAC-SHA-256(PRK, cek_info || 0x01), where cek_info is the ASCII string Content-Encoding: aes128gcm followed by a zero octet. The key is 16 octets.
  • NONCE = HMAC-SHA-256(PRK, nonce_info || 0x01) XOR SEQ, a 12-octet (96-bit) value, where nonce_info is Content-Encoding: nonce plus a zero octet.

SEQ is the record sequence number, a 96-bit unsigned integer in network byte order that starts at zero. Because each record gets a different nonce in a fixed progression, records cannot be removed or reordered without detection.
sections.eli5: Each message gets its own one-time key made by mixing a secret with a random pinch of salt. Every chunk also gets its own number, so shuffling the chunks gives a wrong answer.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The first example encrypts a successful GET response containing the UTF-8 string I am the walrus. It uses a record size of 4096 octets, no padding beyond the delimiter and an empty keyid. The 54-octet body holds a single partial record. The response changes its media type to application/octet-stream to avoid exposing information about the content, or omits Content-Type.

The second example uses a record size of 25 octets, a key identifier of a1 and one zero padding octet in the first record, giving 7 octets of message in the first record and 8 in the second. All binary values are shown in base64url.
sections.eli5: The examples show a real small message being locked up, once in a single envelope and once split across two small envelopes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists several limits of the design:

  • Key and nonce reuse: encrypting different plaintext with the same key and nonce in AES-GCM is not safe. If keying material is reused, the salt MUST be unique each time, and implementations SHOULD generate a random salt per message.
  • Truncation: a receiver can detect truncation. A partially delivered message MUST NOT be processed as though it were complete, for instance cached as complete.
  • Data limits: the total plaintext enciphered under one derived key MUST be less than 2^44.5 blocks of 16 octets. With a record size that is a multiple of 16 octets, that means 398 terabytes. The worst case is a record size of 18 octets, with at most 74 terabytes.
  • Integrity: only content-origin authentication is provided. Anyone with the key can produce content that will be accepted, including all recipients of the same message.
  • Automatic decryption: a receiver may strip the coding unnoticed, so recipients that depend on origin authentication MUST reject messages without the aes128gcm coding.
  • Header leaks and poisoning: only the body is encrypted, so headers such as Content-Type remain visible. A server that accepts an unauthenticated PUT without decrypting it could be poisoned or denied service.
  • Size and timing: message size, timing, methods and URIs can leak information. Padding helps, and distributing non-padding data across records is recommended.
sections.eli5: The locked box hides what is inside, but not the label on the outside or how big the box is. And anyone who has a key can seal a new box that looks genuine.

sections.title: IANA Registration and the JWE Mapping
sections.content:
The RFC registers aes128gcm in the HTTP Content Coding Registry, described as AES-GCM encryption with a 128-bit content-encryption key.

Appendix A shows that the coding can be viewed as a sequence of JSON Web Encryption (JWE, RFC 7516) objects, one per fixed-size record, with a fixed protected header of { "alg": "dir", "enc": "A128GCM" } that is implied by the Content-Encoding header field and not transmitted.
sections.eli5: The name of this coding is written in the official list so everyone agrees what it means.

fields.name: salt
fields.desc: 16 octets. Must be unique per body for the same keying material.

fields.name: rs
fields.desc: Record size in octets. Values smaller than 18 are invalid.

fields.name: idlen
fields.desc: Length of the keyid in octets.

items.title: Data
items.text: Any length up to rs-17 octets of content.

items.title: Delimiter
items.text: 0x01 in every record except the last, which uses 0x02.

items.title: Padding
items.text: Zero octets up to rs-16 (or less in the last record).

items.title: Encrypt
items.text: AEAD_AES_128_GCM adds a 16-octet tag, so the record is rs octets.
